title: Data Security
overview: Data must be kept safe from loss, seen only by the right people, and kept accurate. Paper 1 asks you to distinguish security, privacy and integrity; name and describe threats such as malware, hackers, phishing and pharming; and describe measures that protect the computer system (accounts, passwords, authentication, firewalls, anti-malware) and the data itself (backup, disk mirroring, access rights, encryption). The highest marks go to answers that match a specific measure to a specific threat and say how it reduces the risk.
syllabusPoints: Explain the difference between the terms security, privacy and integrity of data.
Show appreciation of the need for both the security of data and the security of the computer system.

Describe security measures designed to protect computer systems, ranging from the stand-alone PC to a network of computers, including user accounts, passwords, authentication techniques such as digital signatures and biometrics, firewalls, anti-virus software, anti-spyware and encryption.
Show understanding of the threats to computer and data security posed by networks and the internet, including malware (including virus and spyware), hackers, phishing and pharming.
Describe methods that can be used to restrict the risks posed by threats.
Describe security measures designed to protect the security of data, including data backup, disk mirroring, encryption and access rights to data (authorisation).

definitions.definition: Protecting data against loss, damage or corruption, so it is available when needed and can be recovered if lost.
Keeping data available only to authorised users, protecting it from unauthorised access.
The requirement for data to be accurate, complete and up to date, and unchanged except by authorised processes.
Malicious software written with the intention of causing harm to a computer system or the data it holds.
A person who attempts to gain unauthorised access to a computer system.
Sending an email or message that appears to come from a legitimate source in order to trick the recipient into giving away confidential information.
Redirecting a user to a fake website that looks legitimate, for example by altering DNS or browser settings, so that confidential details are entered there.
Verifying that a user is who they claim to be, for example by password, biometrics or a security token.
Defining which files and resources each user may access and what they are allowed to do with them (e.g. read only, read/write).
Hardware or software that monitors incoming and outgoing network traffic and blocks traffic that does not meet a set of rules.
Converting plain text into cipher text using an algorithm and a key, so that intercepted data cannot be understood without the decryption key.
Writing every item of data to two separate disks at the same time, so an identical copy is always available if one disk fails.

sections.title: Security, privacy and integrity of data
content: These three terms are often confused, and examiners reward precise definitions. Data security means the data are protected from being lost or corrupted, so they are available when needed and are the same data that were originally stored. Data privacy means the data can only be seen by people who are authorised to see them. Data integrity means the data are accurate, complete and up to date. Privacy of personal data is supported by data protection laws, which require organisations to keep the data they hold private and accurate and to use them only for the purposes agreed with the individual; the law acts as a deterrent because offenders can be prosecuted.
bullets: Security → protection against loss. Privacy → protection against unauthorised access. Integrity → accuracy.
Security is needed first: lost or corrupted data cannot be private or accurate.
But security alone does not guarantee privacy or integrity; secure data can still be wrong or seen by the wrong people.

examples.label: Two-mark answer: security versus privacy
examples.content:
Question: Describe the difference between the security and the privacy of data. [2]
Mark-scoring answer:
Security is protecting data against loss or corruption. (1)
Privacy is protecting data against access by unauthorised people. (1)

sections.title: Why both the system and the data need protecting
content: Protecting data depends on protecting the computer system that stores it. System security has two aims: to keep the system running and carrying out the tasks users need, and to ensure that only authorised users can access it. Data security measures, such as backups and encryption, then protect the data itself in case the system's defences fail. An organisation needs both: a secure system that is down after a disaster cannot provide its data, and a system that is running but has no backups can lose its data permanently.
bullets: System security measures: user accounts, passwords, authentication, firewalls, anti-malware, disaster recovery planning.
Data security measures: backup, disk mirroring, access rights, encryption.
Threats come from people inside and outside the organisation, from software and from natural disasters.

sections.title: Threats from networks and the internet
content: Threats include careless users, internal mismanagement, natural disasters (fire, flood, earthquake), hackers and malware. A hacker tries to gain unauthorised access, usually by exploiting weaknesses such as weak passwords, unpatched software or out-of-date anti-malware; once in, they may steal, delete or change data, install malware or disrupt the system. Malware takes several forms. A virus attaches itself to other executable code and replicates, corrupting or deleting data. A worm runs independently and spreads itself across a network. A Trojan horse appears to be useful, legitimate software but carries hidden malicious code. Spyware secretly gathers information, such as keystrokes, and sends it to a third party. A logic bomb stays inactive until a condition, such as a date, is met. A bot takes control of a computer so it can be used in attacks on others.
bullets: Phishing: a fake but legitimate-looking email or message persuades the user to reveal confidential details or click a link.
Pharming: malicious code alters DNS or browser settings so a correctly typed web address leads to a fake site.
Keylogging: recording the user's keystrokes to capture passwords and card numbers.
Users often introduce malware accidentally by opening email attachments, downloading files, visiting infected websites or attaching portable storage devices.
Systems have their own weaknesses, such as operating system flaws found after release and buffer overflow, where a program writes beyond the end of a memory buffer and overwrites other data or code.

examples.label: Phishing or pharming?
examples.content:
A bank customer receives an email with the bank's logo asking them to 'confirm their account' using a link → phishing: the user is tricked by a message into acting.
A customer types the bank's correct web address but lands on a copy of the site that records their login → pharming: the redirection happens without any message, because settings or DNS have been tampered with.

sections.title: Restricting the risks posed by threats
content: Each threat has matching preventative measures, and good answers pair them. Against hackers: strong passwords, two-factor authentication, firewalls and keeping software patched. Against malware: up-to-date anti-virus and anti-spyware, a firewall, and restricting which files users can download or run. Against phishing: spam filters, training users to recognise suspicious messages, and never following links in unexpected emails. Against pharming: anti-malware that detects altered settings, and checking that the URL is correct and the site uses HTTPS with a valid certificate. Against natural disasters and system failure: backups stored off site and a disaster recovery plan.
bullets: Organisations can ban or restrict portable storage devices to reduce the risk of malware being brought in.
Software updates (patches) close security holes that attackers exploit.
Good user practice: log off or lock the computer when unattended, do not share or write down passwords, and do not let others watch you log in.

sections.title: Security measures for computer systems
content: Every user should have a user account, which controls what they can do and allows their activity to be logged. Access is protected by authentication. Passwords should be long and use a mix of character types, and are stored in encrypted (hashed) form so that stealing the password file does not reveal them. Biometric methods (fingerprint, face, iris or voice recognition) use a unique physical characteristic that cannot be forgotten or easily copied. Security tokens and one-time codes sent to a phone add a second factor, so a stolen password alone is not enough. A digital signature authenticates the sender of a message and shows it has not been altered. A firewall sits between a network and the internet, checking traffic against rules such as permitted IP addresses and ports and blocking anything not allowed; hardware firewalls protect the whole network while software firewalls protect individual devices. Anti-virus software scans files, attachments and downloads, comparing them with a database of known malware signatures and removing or quarantining threats, so it must be updated regularly; anti-spyware detects and removes spyware in the same way. An intrusion detection system analyses records of system use to spot activity that does not match normal patterns.
bullets: Two-factor authentication combines two different types: something you know (password), something you have (token or phone), something you are (biometric).
Longer passwords with more character types increase the number of combinations an attacker must try.
Disaster recovery planning keeps an organisation running after a major failure, for example by having a remote 'hot site' ready to take over.

examples.label: Why password length matters
examples.content:
There are 95 printable ASCII characters.
8-character passwords: 95^8 ≈ 6.6 × 10^15 combinations
12-character passwords: 95^12 ≈ 5.4 × 10^23 combinations
Each extra character multiplies the number of possibilities by 95, making a brute-force attack far slower.

sections.title: Security measures for data
content: Data can be lost through corrupted or damaged disks, system crashes, accidental deletion or overwriting, as well as through attacks. A backup is a copy of the data made so it can be restored. A typical procedure makes a full backup regularly (such as weekly), keeps at least two generations of full backups, and makes incremental backups of changed data daily, with copies stored off site in a fireproof and flood-proof location. Disk mirroring writes all data to two disks simultaneously, so if one fails the other takes over immediately with no data lost; the second disk can be at a remote site. Access rights (authorisation) give different users different permissions for each file, such as no access, read-only, or read and write, so staff see only the data their role requires. Encryption means that even if data are stolen or intercepted, they cannot be understood without the key.
bullets: Backup protects against loss but the data restored are only as recent as the last backup; mirroring gives an up-to-the-moment copy.
Mirroring does not protect against accidental deletion or malware, because the change is copied to both disks, so backups are still needed.
Encryption does not stop data being stolen or deleted; it stops it being read.
Symmetric encryption uses the same key to encrypt and decrypt; asymmetric encryption uses a public key and a private key (covered fully in topic 17.1).

examples.label: Access rights in a hospital
examples.content:
Doctors: read and write access to their patients' medical records.
Receptionists: read access to appointment details only; no access to medical notes.
IT technicians: access to system settings but no access to patient records.
Each group gets only the access its job requires, protecting patients' privacy.

formulas.label: Password combinations
formulas.expression: number of passwords = (number of possible characters)^(password length)

rows: Gains unauthorised access to steal, change or delete data
Strong passwords, two-factor authentication, firewall, software patches

analysisChains.title: Adding two-factor authentication to staff logins
steps: A user must enter a password and a code from their phone or token
An attacker who has stolen or guessed the password still cannot log in
Phishing attacks that capture passwords become much less useful
But logging in takes longer and users are locked out if they lose their device
analysisChains.evaluation: For systems holding personal or financial data, the extra protection easily outweighs the small inconvenience.

analysisChains.title: Using disk mirroring as well as backups
steps: Every write goes to two disks at the same time
If one disk fails, the other continues immediately with no data lost
The system stays available, which matters for services running 24/7
But deletion or malware damage is mirrored too, so separate backups are still required
analysisChains.evaluation: Mirroring protects against hardware failure and downtime; backups protect against mistakes and attacks. A critical system needs both.

analysisChains.title: Encrypting a laptop's hard drive
steps: All stored data are converted to cipher text
If the laptop is lost or stolen, the thief cannot read the files without the key
The organisation avoids a breach of personal data and possible legal penalties
But if the user forgets the key or password, the data may be unrecoverable
analysisChains.evaluation: Encryption is essential for portable devices holding sensitive data; key management must be planned so data are not lost.

examTips: Use the key words in definitions: security → loss; privacy → unauthorised access; integrity → accuracy.
When asked for a measure, state the measure and explain how it protects against the named threat.
Distinguish phishing (a message tricks the user) from pharming (redirection to a fake site without the user's knowledge).
For access rights, give examples of different levels (no access, read-only, read/write) and link them to user roles.
Say that anti-virus software must be kept up to date, because it relies on a database of known signatures.
commonMistakes: Saying encryption prevents data from being stolen or hacked; it only stops the stolen data being understood.
Saying a firewall removes viruses; it filters network traffic and does not scan files already on the computer.
Treating backups and disk mirroring as the same thing.
Describing data integrity as 'keeping data safe' instead of 'keeping data accurate and up to date'.
Confusing authentication (proving who you are) with authorisation (what you are allowed to access).
Writing 'use a password' without saying it should be strong, changed regularly and kept secret.

quickRecall.question: What is the difference between data security and data privacy?
quickRecall.answer: Security protects data against loss or corruption; privacy protects data against access by unauthorised people.

quickRecall.question: How does a worm differ from a virus?
quickRecall.answer: A worm runs independently and spreads itself across a network; a virus attaches to other executable code to replicate.

quickRecall.question: What is pharming?
quickRecall.answer: Redirecting a user to a fake website, for example by altering DNS or browser settings, so they enter confidential details there.

quickRecall.question: Give two ways of reducing the risk of phishing.
quickRecall.answer: Any two of: spam filters, training users to recognise fake messages, not clicking links in unexpected emails, checking the sender's address.

quickRecall.question: How does a firewall protect a network?
quickRecall.answer: It checks incoming and outgoing traffic against rules and blocks traffic that is not permitted.

quickRecall.question: What is disk mirroring?
quickRecall.answer: Writing data to two disks at the same time, so an identical copy is always available if one disk fails.

quickRecall.question: What is the difference between authentication and authorisation?
quickRecall.answer: Authentication confirms a user's identity; authorisation sets which resources that user may access and what they can do with them.

quickRecall.question: Why must anti-virus software be updated regularly?
quickRecall.answer: It detects malware by comparing files with a database of known signatures, so new malware is missed unless the database is updated.
